title: Targeted search: finding the clients that fit your service for Pressure cleaning (all heights)
audience: Pressure cleaning owners and team leads who want more work from clients that suit their service, their area and their job size.
learningOutcomes: Build a prospect list that is scored against written fit criteria for service area, job size and repeat need.
Identify public signals that a pressure cleaning need may be starting, and explain why each one is a reasonable reason to make contact.
Write a first approach that makes one specific, verifiable observation, offers one small next step and can be declined easily.

instruction.heading: Decide what pressure cleaning work you want before you look for it
instruction.body: Write down the surfaces you do well, the price range you can sustain, the postcodes you can reach without losing money on travel, and how often each kind of client needs you. A route of regular clean-ups, such as common-area paths or a small commercial site, is worth more to a small business than one large job across town. The lead-generation guide's commercial low-rise band is $400 to $2,000, typical $800, for up to three storeys (What's The Damage, verified November 2026), but that is an estimate for the job, not evidence of how often such work is bought.

instruction.heading: Build a scored prospect list, and be plain about the evidence
instruction.body: Keep every candidate in one list with a fit column and a status column. Score each prospect as strong fit, possible fit or not a fit, using written criteria: service area, repeat need, whether you can reach the person who decides, and whether the job falls within your licence and insurance. Candidate segments include owners corporation committees, commercial property managers, real-estate offices and body corporate managers. The research found no evidence of how any of them buy pressure cleaning. Consumer Victoria says an owners corporation manages common property, and lists driveways, pathways, walls, stairwells and gardens as examples, but whether a given surface is common property depends on the plan. Treat each segment as one to test. Use only contact details published for business use, record the date and source of each entry, and do not use bought or harvested lists.

instruction.heading: Watch public tenders and planning registers, for timing only
instruction.body: A public tender or a planning application shows where work is being bought or built. Buying for Victoria lists current and past tenders and lets suppliers set alerts, and each agency publishes an annual plan of what it intends to buy. AusTender does the same at federal level. No pressure-cleaning tender was found in this research, so check the portals for any that appear. Some councils publish planning permit registers with suburb and status fields, such as the City of Casey register on Victoria's open data portal. Check your own council's register. These sources show where to look, not who to contact about a private property. Do not monitor private people, do not enter common property without an invitation, and do not go to a home to make an offer.

instruction.heading: Make a first approach that is specific and easy to decline
instruction.body: A useful first message says how you learned of the tender or notice, makes one specific observation you can verify from public view or the organisation's own published material, and offers one small next step, such as a written quote for one named surface. Keep it short and do not overstate what you know. The ACCC's July 2026 release on unsolicited selling says many approaches were pressured or misleading, and that about 71 per cent of salespeople identified themselves. A specific, honest message that names you is a practical advantage. Where the message goes by email or text, check the consent and unsubscribe rules first.

instruction.heading: Follow up on a fixed schedule and stop when asked
instruction.body: Decide in advance how many follow-ups you will send and how far apart. A common pattern is one reminder after a week and one final message after a further two weeks, then a pause. If a prospect says no or asks you to stop, remove them at once and record the request with its date. At the end of each month, review which fit tier and which signal produced paid work, and move your effort toward them.

procedure: Write the pressure cleaning job, area, price and repeat-need criteria for the work you want.
Build the prospect list and score each entry as strong fit, possible fit or not a fit, with a reason and the source of its contact details.
Choose two or three public signals to watch, such as tender alerts and a council planning register, and note the date each one is seen.
Write one first message for each fit tier, with a stated source, one verifiable observation and one small next step.
Check each message against the electronic message rules and your licence and insurance before sending.
Send to strong-fit prospects first, then follow up on the fixed schedule.
Remove anyone who asks you to stop, and review the results at the end of the month.

workedExamples.situation: A pressure cleaner covers three suburbs. A public tender notice asks for periodic cleaning of paths and forecourts at a small public building in one suburb, and the contact email for the procurement officer is published on the tender page.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Should the owner send a sales message to the procurement officer now, and what should it contain?
workedExamples.reasoning: The owner should read the tender in full first, because the notice sets the scope, the closing date and the rules for contact. A tender notice normally sets how suppliers may ask questions, so the owner reads the notice in full and uses the route it sets, not a cold sales contact (check the notice for its own rules). The owner confirms the scope, capacity and deadline first, and checks that the work is within the licence and insurance held. Any message that does go out names the tender, says how the business learned of it, offers one specific item it can deliver, and asks one question. The owner does not contact residents or staff using private details, and does not enter the site without an invitation.

equipmentAndPpe: Prospect list in a spreadsheet or notebook, with fit and status columns
Written fit criteria for service area, job size and repeat need
Message templates checked against the electronic message rules
No PPE is needed for desk work; any site visit follows the site's own safety rules

commonErrors.error: Sending the same message to everyone on a broad list at once.
commonErrors.prevention: Score the list first, write one message for each fit tier, and start with the strong-fit tier.

commonErrors.error: Using private information about an individual to make contact.
commonErrors.prevention: Use only contact details published for business use, or details the person has given you for this purpose.

commonErrors.error: Pitching a service that you are not licensed or insured to deliver, such as work involving electrical equipment or a roof.
commonErrors.prevention: Check the licence and insurance before outreach, and remove that service from the message.

commonErrors.error: Following up without a limit, or continuing after a request to stop.
commonErrors.prevention: Set a fixed number of follow-ups and a stop rule, and record every stop request.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Do not offer a licensed or authorised service in outreach unless you hold the licence that the state or territory where the work is done requires. No licence for pressure cleaning was found in this research. Licence rules differ between states and territories, so check each one you work in. This lesson does not grant any licence.

Commercial electronic messages, including email and text, are regulated by the Spam Act 2003 (Cth). ACMA's guidance says marketing messages need consent, that consent should be recorded, and that unsubscribe requests must be honoured within five working days. ACMA's Spam Act obligations page (last updated 28 March 2019) says the Act also covers business addresses, and that publishing an address does not by itself permit commercial messages. The Act text was not read for this lesson.

Public information does not by itself permit contact about anything. If the Privacy Act applies to your business, OAIC's guidance on direct marketing says public information is not exempt from the direct-marketing rules. Whether the Act applies to a small business is unconfirmed here. Use only contact details published for business use, keep them secure, and stop using them when someone objects.
Victoria: runoff and working-at-height rules for outreach-led site work were not checked. Check them with EPA Victoria and WorkSafe Victoria before quoting a site.

qualityStandard: Every prospect on the list has a fit score, a reason for that score and a recorded source for its contact details.
Every first message contains one verifiable observation and one small, easy-to-decline next step.
No contact is made using private information, and every stop request is recorded and actioned.
documentationEvidence: Prospect list with fit score, reason, status, source and date added.
Signal log with the date each public signal was seen.
Stop-request record with the date it was actioned.
summary: Define the pressure cleaning work you want first, then filter prospects against that definition.
Watch public tenders and registers for timing, and never use private information to make contact.
Keep the first approach specific and easy to decline, and stop when asked. Owners corporation and commercial prospects are untested for pressure work.

knowledgeChecks.question: Which prospect should you contact first?
options: A one-off job well outside your service area, because it looks large
A property group with several sites inside your service area that you already visit
Any business that has a website, because it probably spends money on services

knowledgeChecks.question: A public tender asks for paths and forecourts to be cleaned at a building in your area. What is the most appropriate first step?
options: Read the tender in full and contact the buyer only by the route the notice sets and the electronic message and do-not-call rules allow
Message each resident using their private contact details and ask them to sign up for the cleaning
Go into the site to look at the paths before making contact and ask the crew what they are doing

knowledgeChecks.question: Before you send a commercial email to a prospect, what should you do?
options: Check that the message is short enough to read on a phone and it has a fun subject line
Ask the prospect to like your social media page first and then send the message
Confirm the Spam Act 2003 requirements in current ACMA guidance before sending

officialReferences.title: Avoid sending spam (ACMA)
officialReferences.covers: Read 2026-11-03: a business needs consent before sending marketing messages, and consent must be recorded; each message must identify the sender and include contact details for at least 30 days; every commercial message must include a free unsubscribe option that works for at least 30 days and is honoured within 5 working days. Does not cover privacy law. Publisher: ACMA.

officialReferences.title: Australian Privacy Principles guidelines (OAIC)
officialReferences.covers: Read 2026-11-03: the APPs apply to organisations covered by the Privacy Act, which covers organisations with an annual turnover of more than $3 million and some others. The page as read lists the APP chapters only; small-business coverage and consent detail are UNCONFIRMED. Publisher: OAIC.
